props.title: Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein
props.initialSlug: Comedy duo faces classic Universal monsters

sections.content: Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein brilliantly bridges classic Universal horror with comedy, creating the template for horror-comedy crossovers. Bud Abbott and Lou Costello's perfectly-timed vaudeville routines clash magnificently with Bela Lugosi reprising his iconic Dracula role and Lon Chaney Jr. returning as The Wolf Man. The film's genius lies in treating its monsters deadly seriously while letting the comedy flow naturally from Abbott and Costello's reactions. This approach influenced everything from The Ghost Breakers (1940) to Ghostbusters (1984).

sections.content: The success of Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein launched a whole series of monster meetings, including Abbott and Costello Meet the Killer, Boris Karloff (1949) and Abbott and Costello Meet the Mummy (1955). These films preserved Universal's monster legacy while introducing them to new audiences through comedy. The formula proved so successful that it influenced later horror-comedies like An American Werewolf in London (1981) and Shaun of the Dead (2004), which maintain serious horror elements while mining laughs from their characters' reactions.

What makes the film particularly special is how it serves as a legitimate entry in both Universal's monster canon and Abbott and Costello's comedy series. Lugosi's Dracula is just as menacing as in Dracula (1931), while Chaney Jr.'s tortured Wolf Man maintains all the pathos from The Wolf Man (1941). Meanwhile, Abbott and Costello deliver some of their best routines, including the famous moving candle scene and Costello's gradual realization that he's dealing with real monsters. sections.content: The film's impact on horror-comedy can't be overstated. It proved that scares and laughs could coexist without undermining either, influencing films like Evil Dead II (1987) and Tremors (1990). Modern filmmakers like Sam Raimi and Peter Jackson have cited it as a major influence, with Jackson's The Frighteners (1996) particularly showing its DNA. The film also marked the last time Bela Lugosi would play Dracula on screen, giving it additional historical significance.
